text: The domestic space here is doing double duty -- the hacienda is both a literal house and a record of the labor relations that produced it. Renata's position as a woman professional entering a feminized domestic space with masculinized tools of measurement creates a productive tension the story doesn't resolve neatly. She can't contain the house in her report any more than the 1894 real estate listing could contain the workers' quarters. That parallel is the story's sharpest move. The Beatriz subplot is brief but devastating: a woman who stops leaving the house, whose complexion takes on 'the color of the local stone,' consumed by the space she was supposed to inhabit as mistress. The priest dismisses her as impressionable, recommends less novel-reading. A familiar pattern. I'd push back slightly on the underground room sequence, which edges toward body horror in a way that feels like a different story. But the line 'there is no field for what I experienced' might be the most precise articulation of institutional erasure I've read in horror fiction.
